questions.stem: Historians often call the slow-growth years under Leonid Brezhnev in the 1970s and early 1980s:
options: the era of stagnation
the Khrushchev thaw
the New Economic Policy
the Great Turn
questions.explanation: Under Brezhnev growth slowed, technology lagged behind the West and corruption spread, a period later labelled the era of stagnation. The thaw was Khrushchev's relaxation after Stalin, and the New Economic Policy belongs to the 1920s.

questions.stem: Under Soviet central planning, factories were judged mainly on meeting output targets set in Moscow. A common result by the 1980s was that:
options: factories produced large surpluses of high-quality consumer goods for export
prices rose rapidly because firms competed to attract customers
managers closed unprofitable plants and laid off their workers
goods met quantity targets but were often poor quality or unwanted
questions.explanation: Planners rewarded the quantity produced, so enterprises had little reason to improve quality, innovate or respond to what consumers wanted. Prices were fixed by the state, not set by competition, and unprofitable plants were kept open.

questions.stem: Why did the Soviet Union's very high defence spending weaken its economy in the 1980s?
options: it took resources and skilled workers away from civilian industry
it forced the government to cut the size of the armed forces by half each year
it was paid for by selling state factories to Western investors
it caused the Soviet republics to stop paying taxes to Moscow
questions.explanation: Matching the United States militarily absorbed a large share of a smaller economy, leaving less for housing, consumer goods and modern civilian technology. The USSR did not sell factories to Western investors to pay for it.

questions.stem: The sharp fall in world oil prices in the mid-1980s hurt the Soviet Union mainly because:
options: the USSR imported most of the oil it needed from countries in the Middle East
lower prices forced the closure of all Soviet oilfields in Western Siberia
oil was the main fuel used to feed the Soviet Union's livestock herds
oil exports earned the hard currency it used to import grain and machinery
questions.explanation: The USSR was a major oil exporter, and oil and gas sales paid for imported grain, food and Western technology. When prices fell, this income shrank just as Gorbachev's reforms began, adding to shortages and foreign debt.

questions.stem: Historians see the war in Afghanistan as a contributing cause of the Soviet collapse because it:
options: led the United States to declare war on the Soviet Union in the early 1980s
forced the Soviet government to stop all military spending until 1989
drained resources and, under glasnost, damaged the regime's prestige
ended with Afghanistan joining the Soviet Union as its sixteenth union republic
questions.explanation: The war was costly and unwinnable, and returning veterans and an increasingly open press exposed its human cost. It weakened confidence in the army and the party. Afghanistan never became a Soviet republic.

questions.stem: Three elderly General Secretaries died in office between 1982 and 1985. This sequence is significant to the end of the Soviet Union mainly because it:
options: allowed the republics to elect their own leaders without Moscow's approval
caused the immediate collapse of Soviet control in Eastern Europe
helped persuade the Politburo to choose a younger reformer
led the party to abolish the position of General Secretary in 1985
questions.explanation: The rule of ailing old men symbolised a system that had stopped renewing itself. In 1985 the Politburo chose Gorbachev, then 54, and his reforms set the events of 1985 to 1991 in motion. The post of General Secretary continued until 1991.

questions.stem: The Russian word perestroika, the name of Gorbachev's central reform program, means:
options: restructuring
openness
acceleration
democratisation
questions.explanation: Perestroika meant restructuring of the economy and, later, the political system. Openness is glasnost, acceleration is uskoreniye and democratisation was a separate slogan, demokratizatsiya.

questions.stem: The Law on State Enterprise (1987) gave managers more freedom over wages and output, and the Law on Cooperatives (1988) allowed small private businesses. Prices, however, stayed largely controlled. Many historians argue the result was:
options: the full return of Stalin-style central planning and collectivisation
a stable mixed economy that lasted unchanged into the 1990s
more money chasing scarce goods, so shortages and the deficit grew
a rapid rise in consumer goods that ended queues in Soviet shops by 1989
questions.explanation: Partial reform loosened control over wages and enterprise money without letting prices adjust or creating real markets. Incomes rose faster than the supply of goods, so shortages grew and the state's finances deteriorated. This is a key argument for reform itself as a cause of collapse.

questions.stem: The explosion at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant in Ukraine on 26 April 1986 is linked to glasnost because:
options: it led Gorbachev to end glasnost and restore full censorship of the press for several years
it was caused by Western saboteurs, which united the Soviet people behind their government
the secretive official response discredited secrecy and led Gorbachev to widen glasnost
it was the first disaster the Soviet government reported to its people within the same hour
questions.explanation: Officials delayed telling the public and the world, and the damage to trust was severe. Gorbachev drew the lesson that secrecy was dangerous and extended glasnost. It also fed environmental and national protest in Ukraine and Belarus.

questions.stem: Why did glasnost weaken the Communist Party's authority in the late 1980s?
options: revelations of past crimes and present failures undermined the party's legitimacy
it banned all criticism of the party, which caused protests across the Soviet Union
it transferred control of the newspapers to the KGB, which turned against the party
it gave the Soviet republics full control over foreign policy and the armed forces
questions.explanation: Newspapers, books and television revealed Stalin's terror, the secret 1939 Nazi-Soviet Pact, corruption and economic failure. Once citizens could say what they thought, the party's claim to legitimacy and its official version of history collapsed.

questions.stem: In March 1989 Soviet citizens voted in the first competitive national elections since 1917. They elected the:
options: Council of Ministers
Politburo of the party
Congress of People's Deputies
State Duma of Russia
questions.explanation: The Congress of People's Deputies was created by Gorbachev's political reforms of 1988. Many party officials were defeated, and the televised sessions, where critics such as Andrei Sakharov spoke, gripped the country.

questions.stem: In 1990 the Soviet constitution was amended to remove Article 6. This article had:
options: allowed the army to intervene in Eastern European countries
guaranteed the Communist Party's leading role in Soviet society
given each of the union republics the right to leave the Soviet Union
made Russian the only official language of the Soviet Union
questions.explanation: Removing Article 6 ended the party's constitutional monopoly on power and opened the way for other parties. The right of republics to secede was a separate provision that stayed in the constitution and was used by independence movements.

questions.stem: A historian describes Gorbachev's reforms as a paradox. Which statement best explains this view?
options: measures meant to open the economy led to the return of collectivisation
measures meant to revive socialism released criticism and forces that destroyed it
measures meant to end the Cold War made the arms race with the United States much faster
measures meant to strengthen the republics gave Moscow total control over them
questions.explanation: Gorbachev wanted a more efficient, humane socialism, not the end of the Soviet Union. But openness and democratisation removed the fear and control that had held the system together. The Cold War in fact eased under his leadership.

questions.stem: The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty, signed by Gorbachev and Reagan in December 1987, was the first agreement to:
options: eliminate a whole class of nuclear weapons
ban nuclear weapons tests in the atmosphere
set up a hotline between the superpowers
dissolve the Warsaw Pact and NATO
questions.explanation: The INF Treaty removed all US and Soviet ground-launched missiles with ranges of 500 to 5,500 kilometres. The atmospheric test ban dated from 1963 and the hotline from 1963. Easing the arms race let Gorbachev hope to divert resources to the economy.

questions.stem: In a speech to the United Nations in December 1988, Gorbachev:
options: declared that the Brezhnev Doctrine would be applied to any satellite state that rebelled
announced a one-sided cut of 500,000 troops and backed freedom of choice for nations
announced that Soviet forces would stay in Eastern Europe as long as NATO existed
demanded that the United States withdraw its forces from Western Europe within a year
questions.explanation: Gorbachev announced unilateral reductions in Soviet forces and said that nations should be free to choose their own path. Eastern European reformers read this as a signal that the Soviet army would not prop up their regimes.

questions.stem: How did the fall of communist governments in Eastern Europe in 1989 contribute to the end of the Soviet Union itself?
options: it showed the republics that Moscow would not use full force, encouraging their demands
it led the new Eastern European governments to send troops into the Baltic republics in 1990
it caused the Soviet Union to annex East Germany as a new union republic
it ended Soviet trade with Eastern Europe, which had supplied most of its oil
questions.explanation: The peaceful revolutions in Poland, Hungary, East Germany and Czechoslovakia were watched closely in the Baltic states, Ukraine and the Caucasus. If the outer empire could leave, so might the republics, and hardliners blamed Gorbachev for 'losing' Eastern Europe.

questions.stem: On 23 August 1989 about two million people formed the Baltic Way, a human chain through Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. It marked the 50th anniversary of:
options: the death of Stalin and the start of the thaw in Soviet cultural life
the 1939 Nazi-Soviet Pact that led to Soviet occupation of the Baltic states
the end of the Second World War in Europe and the liberation of the Baltic states
the founding of the Warsaw Pact alliance by the Soviet Union and its allies
questions.explanation: The pact's secret protocols placed the Baltic states in the Soviet sphere, and they were annexed in 1940. Glasnost had allowed the protocols to be discussed openly, and the chain demanded recognition that the annexation was illegal.

questions.stem: Which union republic was the first to declare its independence from the Soviet Union, on 11 March 1990?
options: Georgia
Kazakhstan
Lithuania
Ukraine
questions.explanation: Lithuania's Supreme Council declared independence in March 1990, and Moscow responded with an economic blockade. Ukraine declared independence only after the August 1991 coup, and Kazakhstan was the last republic to do so, in December 1991.

questions.stem: In January 1991 Soviet troops killed civilians at the television tower in Vilnius, Lithuania, but Moscow did not go on to crush the independence movement. This episode best illustrates that:
options: the Lithuanian independence movement collapsed once troops were deployed
Western governments approved of the use of force to hold the union together
limited force discredited Gorbachev with reformers but did not restore control
Gorbachev had decided to restore Stalin's methods of rule throughout the union
questions.explanation: The killings outraged Lithuanians, Russian democrats and Western governments, and Gorbachev distanced himself from them. Half-hearted force left him blamed by reformers for the violence and by hardliners for weakness, while Lithuania's resolve hardened.

questions.stem: In June 1990 the Russian republic, led by Boris Yeltsin, declared its sovereignty. This was significant because:
options: Russia agreed to give up its seat on the United Nations Security Council
Yeltsin used it to make the Communist Party the only legal political party in Russia
it placed all of the other republics under direct rule from Russia
the largest republic now claimed that its laws overrode those of the Soviet Union
questions.explanation: When Russia, the heart of the union, asserted its own sovereignty, the centre lost its main base of support. A 'war of laws' followed between Russian and Soviet institutions, with Yeltsin and Gorbachev competing for authority.

questions.stem: Why did Boris Yeltsin's election as President of Russia in June 1991 strengthen him against Gorbachev?
options: Yeltsin's election made him commander of all Soviet forces in place of Gorbachev
Yeltsin's election made Russia the only republic allowed to collect Soviet taxes
Yeltsin was chosen by popular vote, while Gorbachev had been elected only by the Congress
Yeltsin was chosen by the Politburo, while Gorbachev had been elected by the republics' leaders
questions.explanation: Gorbachev had been made President of the USSR in 1990 by the Congress of People's Deputies and never faced a popular vote. Yeltsin's direct mandate gave him legitimacy Gorbachev lacked, which mattered greatly during the August coup.

questions.stem: The hardliners who tried to seize power in August 1991 called themselves the:
options: State Committee on the State of Emergency
Committee for State Security
Council of the Republics
Congress of People's Deputies
questions.explanation: The committee included Vice-President Yanayev, KGB chief Kryuchkov and Defence Minister Yazov. The Committee for State Security was the KGB itself, whose chairman took part, not the name of the group.

questions.stem: The main aim of the plotters in August 1991 was to:
options: force Gorbachev to speed up the transition to a full market economy by 1992
hand power to Boris Yeltsin as the elected leader of Russia
take the Soviet Union into NATO as quickly as possible
stop the signing of a new Union Treaty giving power to the republics
questions.explanation: The new treaty, due to be signed on 20 August, would have turned the USSR into a looser federation. The plotters held Gorbachev at his holiday house at Foros in Crimea and declared a state of emergency to prevent it.

questions.stem: Which best explains why the August 1991 coup collapsed within three days?
options: Gorbachev escaped from Crimea and personally led loyal army units back into Moscow
NATO forces crossed the border and threatened to occupy Moscow
the plotters handed power to the Baltic republics in exchange for support
Yeltsin led resistance at the Russian parliament and key army units refused to act
questions.explanation: Yeltsin climbed onto a tank outside the Russian parliament building to denounce the coup, crowds gathered to defend it, and commanders would not order troops to fire on them. The plotters lost their nerve. Gorbachev was released, not rescued by his own troops.

questions.stem: Which was a direct consequence of the failed August 1991 coup?
options: Gorbachev was elected President of the Soviet Union
Article 6 of the Soviet constitution was removed
Ukraine's parliament declared independence within days
Lithuania made its first declaration of independence
questions.explanation: Ukraine declared independence on 24 August 1991, and other republics followed. Yeltsin also suspended the Communist Party's activity in Russia. Lithuania's declaration, Gorbachev's election as President and the removal of Article 6 all came in 1990.

questions.stem: On 1 December 1991 more than 90 per cent of Ukrainian voters supported independence. Historians such as Serhii Plokhy see this vote as decisive because:
options: it was the first time any Soviet citizens had voted in a referendum
it made Ukraine the legal successor to the Soviet Union at the UN
it was followed by a Russian invasion that ended the union
Russia's leaders would not keep a union in which Ukraine was absent
questions.explanation: Independence won a majority in every region, including the Russian-speaking east and Crimea. Yeltsin would not join a union without Ukraine, and a week later the Belavezha Accords declared the USSR at an end. Russia, not Ukraine, took the Soviet seat at the United Nations.

questions.stem: On 8 December 1991 the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus signed the Belavezha Accords, which:
options: created a new Union Treaty that kept a single Soviet army and a single Soviet currency for all republics
restored Gorbachev as leader of a reformed Communist Party of the Soviet Union
admitted the three Baltic states into a new federation led by Russia and Ukraine
declared that the USSR had ceased to exist and created the Commonwealth of Independent States
questions.explanation: Yeltsin, Kravchuk and Shushkevich met near Brest in Belarus and replaced the union with a loose Commonwealth of Independent States. Eight more republics joined at Alma-Ata on 21 December. The Baltic states never joined.

questions.stem: What happened on 25 December 1991?
options: the Berlin Wall was opened and East Germans crossed freely to the West
the last Soviet troops left Afghanistan across the Amu Darya river
Gorbachev resigned as President and the Soviet flag was lowered over the Kremlin
Yeltsin stood on a tank to defy the hardliners outside the Russian parliament
questions.explanation: Gorbachev announced his resignation on television, and the Russian flag replaced the Soviet flag over the Kremlin that evening. The Soviet parliament formally dissolved the union the next day. The tank was in August 1991 and the Wall opened in November 1989.

questions.stem: In 'The Gorbachev Factor' (1996), Archie Brown argues that the most important reason for the changes of 1985-1991 was:
options: American military pressure, which forced the Soviet economy into bankruptcy
nationalist risings that had been planned before Gorbachev took office
the fall in world oil prices, which made collapse certain by 1986
Gorbachev's own choices, since the system showed no sign of imminent collapse
questions.explanation: Brown argues that despite deep problems the USSR could have continued for years, and that Gorbachev's decisions to reform and not to use force transformed it. This is an interpretation stressing individual agency rather than structural forces.

questions.stem: Stephen Kotkin's 'Armageddon Averted' (2001) explains the Soviet collapse mainly by:
options: the military defeat of the Soviet army by Afghan resistance fighters in the late 1980s
the system's failure to compete with the West and the elite's choice not to use force
the Reagan administration's arms build-up, which he sees as the single decisive cause of collapse
a carefully planned campaign by Western intelligence agencies to break up the Soviet Union
questions.explanation: Kotkin stresses that Soviet socialism had lost the economic competition with the West, and that the elite, despite having vast coercive power, did not use it to save the union, so the end was largely peaceful. He plays down US military spending as the cause.

questions.stem: Yegor Gaidar, a Russian economist and minister in the 1990s, argued in 'Collapse of an Empire' that the Soviet collapse was largely a story of:
options: a war over oil with neighbouring states in the Middle East
the deliberate sale of Soviet oilfields to American companies
grain imports that the state paid for with oil revenue that then fell
a revolt by collective farmers who refused to grow grain after 1985
questions.explanation: Gaidar argued that the USSR came to depend on imported grain, paid for with oil exports. When oil prices fell in the 1980s, the state ran short of hard currency and borrowed heavily, and its economic base gave way.

questions.stem: Mark Beissinger argues that between 1987 and 1991 the break-up of the USSR went from seeming impossible to seeming inevitable. He explains this mainly through:
options: the votes of the United Nations General Assembly in favour of independence
a 'tide' of nationalist protest in which each movement's success encouraged others
long-planned uprisings in every republic that were all launched on the same day
the decision of the Russian army to divide the union between its commanders
questions.explanation: Beissinger shows that national identities and demands changed quickly as protest spread from republic to republic, each success making the next more likely. He rejects the idea that the nations were simply waiting to break free.

questions.stem: A historian wants to challenge the 'triumphalist' view that United States pressure brought down the Soviet Union. Which evidence would best support the challenge?
options: In the early 1980s the United States greatly increased its spending on defence
In the 1980s the United States supplied weapons to resistance fighters in Afghanistan
In August 1991 President Bush warned Ukrainians in Kyiv against 'suicidal nationalism'
In 1983 President Reagan announced the Strategic Defense Initiative to destroy missiles
questions.explanation: Bush's Kyiv speech shows that Washington wanted the union kept together, fearing civil war and loose nuclear weapons, which Plokhy uses to argue that the republics, not the US, ended it. The other three items are evidence for US pressure, so they support the triumphalist view.

questions.stem: Vladislav Zubok's 'Collapse' (2021) differs from structural explanations because it argues that:
options: the Soviet Union was brought down mainly by NATO's expansion in the 1980s
the collapse was caused mainly by the Chernobyl disaster and its cost
the collapse was not inevitable and came largely from Gorbachev's own decisions
the Soviet Union had been bound to collapse ever since the Bolshevik revolution of 1917
questions.explanation: Zubok argues that Gorbachev's economic and political choices, such as loosening financial control and avoiding firm action, created the crisis, and that a different course could have kept a reformed union. Structural accounts see the system's weaknesses as making collapse very likely.

questions.stem: A historian uses Gorbachev's memoirs, published after 1991, to explain his decisions. What is the main limitation of this source?
options: memoirs cannot tell us anything about a leader's intentions
it was written before most of the events of 1991 took place
Gorbachev wrote with hindsight and had reason to defend his record
Gorbachev was not present at the main events he describes
questions.explanation: Memoirs give an insider's view of motives and debates, which makes them useful. But they are written after the event by people who want to justify themselves, so claims must be checked against documents and other witnesses.

questions.stem: A 1984 article in Pravda, the Communist Party newspaper, reports that the Soviet economy is meeting its plan targets. For a historian of the economy, this source is most useful as evidence of:
options: the real state of the Soviet economy in the early 1980s
the views of ordinary consumers queuing in Soviet shops
the opinions of Western economists about Soviet growth
the official picture the party wished to present before glasnost
questions.explanation: Before glasnost the press was controlled and published the party line, so the article reliably shows what the regime wanted people to believe. It is unreliable as a measure of actual economic performance, which official statistics often overstated.

questions.stem: A Lithuanian independence leaflet from 1990 and a confidential report by Communist Party officials in Moscow both describe huge crowds at independence rallies in Vilnius. Why does this agreement strengthen the evidence?
options: official party reports were always more accurate than any other source
leaflets are primary sources and so cannot exaggerate the size of a crowd
sources with opposing perspectives and purposes corroborate the same claim
both sources were written by the same author for the same audience
questions.explanation: The nationalists had reason to exaggerate support and party officials had reason to play it down. When both agree that crowds were huge, the claim is far more credible. Neither type of source is automatically reliable.

questions.stem: Many historians writing after 1991 revised earlier accounts of the Soviet collapse. The main reason was that:
options: Soviet party and state archives became far more accessible to researchers
all Western historians were banned from writing about the Soviet Union until then
the Soviet government had destroyed every record of the Gorbachev years
the events were too recent for anyone to have written about them before 1991
questions.explanation: Access to Politburo records, other archives and frank interviews let historians test claims about Gorbachev's intentions and the coup. This changes the nature and range of evidence available, a key issue in historiography.

questions.stem: Under the Budapest Memorandum of 1994, Ukraine gave up the nuclear weapons it had inherited from the Soviet Union in return for:
options: a promise of immediate membership of NATO and the European Union
the transfer of Crimea from Russian to Ukrainian rule
a permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council
security assurances from Russia, the United States and Britain
questions.explanation: The assurances included respect for Ukraine's existing borders. Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014, the end point of the syllabus topic, broke them and is often cited when debating the unfinished legacy of the Soviet break-up. Crimea was already part of Ukraine in 1991.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a continuity between the end of the Soviet Union and the Russo-Ukrainian War that began in 2014?
options: the continued membership of all fifteen republics in the Warsaw Pact
Ukraine's rejection of independence in its 1991 referendum
disputes over borders and the status of Russian speakers left in new states
the Communist Party's return to power in Moscow immediately after 1991
questions.explanation: When the USSR dissolved along republic borders, millions of Russians and Russian speakers lived in other new states, and Crimea, with its naval base, stayed in Ukraine. These issues resurfaced in 2014. The Warsaw Pact had dissolved in 1991.
